utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in a Status Conference. We just want to look at the progress and review the status of the case and also discuss the facilities for Mr. Milan Simic. I'll start with the Prosecution. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. If Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: After this witness, how many more witnesses? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. My calculation is that we have 31 witnesses remaining. Of those witnesses, one is Ewa Tabeau, who is in the nature of an expert, demographics expert. And two of them are witnesses who will give evidence on the issue of international armed conflict. The remainder are all fact witnesses, describing events in and around the municipality. Thus far, we have completed, I believe, about -- yes, 15 witnesses. So we're about a third of the way through our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It appears we have a long way to go. MR. DI FAZIO: It does. I regret to say, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because the remaining days we can only sit either mornings or afternoon, which diminishes the sitting hours. MR. DI FAZIO: If it's any consolation to the Chamber and to my learned friends, and to us, of course, I think the issues are slowly narrowing down. And as we get into the case further, I think the witnesses hopefully will become shorter and shorter as we focus more and more on the more crucial issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because I was just about to say that narrowing down on the issues and also looking at where you think the vacuums may be and filling in -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. The Prosecution is acutely aware of that. We're well aware of the fact that the Chamber wants us to do whatever possible to limit the evidence. And we are, I think, using our best efforts to just get out the essential stuff out of each witness. Unfortunately, that can't really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. We -- MR. DI FAZIO: -- do a dramatic short of shortening --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber doesn't want to put undue pressure, because we are aware of the problems we've had in this case and the fact that it's actually four trials in one going on at the same time. MR. DI FAZIO: Not only that, if Your Honours please, not only that, but it's the sort of case that involves evidence of events over months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: It's not one particular shooting. It's not a camp. Just because of that, it's just, of necessary, the witnesses have to give lengthier evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Now I turn to the Defence counsel for Mr. Milan Simic. I wanted to find out how far -- so far how are the facilities of the videolink.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as the video set-up, everything is fine. Our client says that he can see everything fine and he can hear everything. And that's great. There is just one slight problem. We're having a problem with the communication on the phone. We can call him, no problem, but he informed us today that he's having a hard time reaching us when he wants to reach us. He has reached us in the last couple of days, but there have been times he says when he can't get a hold of us when he needs to. So I'm sure that's not going to be a huge problem. We can iron all that out. But right now it is a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Maybe -- I'm not sure how -- whether there is somebody from the technical unit at the Detention Unit to help him with getting through the line. But I think that will be taken up by the Registrar's Office, the people who are making these arrangements, because that is important that he should be able to communicate with counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because if the facilities are fine, he's able to follow the proceedings -- he's able to follow the proceedings, he can see who the witnesses are and get information on their identity, then it wouldn't be that necessary for him to come into the courtroom whenever he feels like not sitting in his wheelchair for too long.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Well, I knew we were going to address this issue. And I -- I think the whole object here is nobody wants to be here in this trial longer than we have to be. In fact, I wish this trial would have been over last December. But I know that we're starting increased hours next Monday, till 7.00. And that's no problem, obviously, if my client is in the jail, lying down, watching the trial. That's not problem. But there are -- there are going to be maybe a couple of witnesses for the Prosecution where he is going to want to be here in the courtroom. And so I don't want in any way to suggest to the Chamber that this videolink is a substitute for his presence here in the courtroom. It is a matter of convenience, which we really appreciate, and it's going to allow us to have this trial go a lot faster, I think. We'll get that extra hour. But I know that under Article 21 of the Statute, he's entitled to be present here in the courtroom. And so I don't want to in any way say that it's a substitute for him being present here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. It's a question of him, if he is unwell and he's in the Detention Unit, he's able to follow the proceedings, because that is important.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Exactly. I think we are all on the same page, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So once the telephone problem is sorted out, then there should be an improvement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And I do want to say this. We, our team, really appreciates all the efforts that have gone to help us in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because what is important on the part of the people running the -- operating the videolink is that they would like to be informed, at the latest, a day in advance, so it is important that you keep a close communication with your client and you also observe the type of witnesses who are coming so that you can give him advice correctly as to whether or not he can take a decision on being in the courtroom and not being in the Detention Unit. Because there is also the transport unit who also need advance notice.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as long as we keep having a week's notice on the order of witnesses, we can give a couple of days notice to everybody who needs to know whether or not he wants to be here. But this does raise another issue, actually, and it's not so much our problem as it is the Prosecution's problem. And today with this witness, I think this witness is going to testify about our client, and the Prosecution is -- we've got to come up with some solution. If they want identification evidence regarding our client, they're going to have to come up with some solution. And we're happy to work with them. As a matter of fact, for the last witness, Mrs. Delic, we waived any identification issues. I haven't had a chance to discuss this witness, whether or not our client will waive that. I don't know -- that's just going to be a problem because this is a weird -- this is a strange situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It's a criminal trial, yes, and we have to be aware of the rights of accused. It's just that with the facilities being provided, then there shouldn't be that much pressure on Mr. Milan Simic. Because what I'm trying to avoid is a total breakdown of his health, because that will mean adjourning the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: He isn't -- his health isn't very good, but actually, it's remaining more stable now that he's able --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He's able to rest, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Yes. But what I'm talking about right now is a different issue about the Prosecution's problem which I can find out whether or not he's going to waive that evidence for this witness on Monday. But it might be a continuing problem. If there are a few more witnesses dealing with the primary school or whatever, we need to address that legally. I don't know if they want to think about some kind of photo spread, if he doesn't weigh that issue or not. But I just want to let everybody know we are willing to discuss anything to make this trial go faster and not have any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That will be very helpful. That will be very helpful. And the Trial Chamber would like to thank the Registrar's Office and the Deputy Registrar's Office for these facilities because they're really gone a long way in assisting us to get through with our trial. Yes. For Monday, the hours will change. We shall be sitting up to 19.00, like the programme which has been issued. And we have also issued a table of the UN holidays when the Chamber will not be sitting, because the programme simply shows as if we are sitting on all the days. But on those UN holidays, the Chamber will not be sitting. So were going to -- Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may -- well, allow me to say, even within this high-tech institution there are sometimes problem with telephone lines, what we can say for Samac in wartime. But anyhow, something which my learned friend Mr. Di Fazio just stated was not so clear for me. In fact, we have a close --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In fact, we have a close list of witnesses to my evidence, including Mr. Delicic and Ms. Tabeau, the other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. What was not clear to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I don't see particular names on this list for witnesses for international armed conflict. Maybe my learned friend can clarify that. Who are the witnesses? Maybe they are here. I'm a little bit confused about this submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure that can be clarified between the parties by the Prosecution merely indicating which witness is discussing what. But the Trial Chamber is aware that summaries were given to the Defence counsel, but sometimes maybe you just need more details about what type of witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But I'm speaking -- yeah, I'm speaking about the list provided by the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: For next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Prior to trial. Generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And I'm a little bit lost in this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- document. But okay. I appreciate your suggestion. Of course we can -- we can communicate by -- between us. And if we would have enough time, maybe a couple of minutes, maybe I can raise another issue at the discretion of this Trial Chamber, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I think it would just be helpful also for the Trial Chamber to know that the two witnesses Mr. Di Fazio referred to as the international armed conflict witnesses are those whose testimony was admitted pursuant to a 92 bis motion. Their evidence was admitted by the Pre-Trial Chamber subject to cross-examination. And it's that context -- that's what we meant. So they're not on the summaries, but they're those two -- those two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now I remember, because there was a hearing about the witnesses. I think one is a former colonel of JNA and -- yes, I know now. Thank you so much, Ms. Reidy. And if you allow me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, there is one practice which is not so clear for the Defence, I mean, a practice from the side of Prosecution. I will give you an example, and I would be very glad if our learned friends can clarify that. Just for the record, I have to say that on the 18th February 2002, the Prosecution submitted to the Defence a transcript with Mr. Stevan Todorovic -- transcript of his interview, which was -- which took place on 30 July 2001. So from July 2001 until the February 2002, the Prosecutor was in possession of this particular interview. As a matter of principle, I think that this practice should not be allowed in future. And furthermore, I think officially move this Honourable Trial Chamber to strike out this evidence because they were in possession well prior to trial, the beginning of the trial. And another thing: On the 18th of February this year, our colleagues from Prosecution gave us sort of -- they called it proofing notes or something like that, an extended version of the -- of the interview with Mr. Stevan Todorovic. And when I asked my learned friend Mr. Di Fazio to inform me where and when this proofing notes were made, on which occasions, still up to now we don't have these answers. So maybe my learned friend Mr. Di Fazio can, for the record, inform Defence and this Trial Chamber when and where, on which occasion, these proofing notes were made, because it is very important for the Defence in order to check certain details, to arrange defence, and stuff like that. And also maybe he can give us an explanation why he gave to the Defence this transcript of 30 of July last year only in February this year. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: First of all, on the transcript of Mr. Todorovic given to the Defence on 18 February, there is nothing the Trial Chamber can strike out because it hasn't yet been offered as evidence. So those are simply documents which the parties are exchanging in preparation -- in the event that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, that is the main issue. I'm not speaking whether this evidence will be tendered or proved or whatever. I'm speaking about the manner of the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which means that -- you can understand. If I would be as a Defence in position to have this, for example, interview prior to the beginning of trial, maybe I can use that during the cross-examination of the -- all witnesses that came. And my -- my basic concern is about the possible jeopardising of the principle of fairness in this trial. That, I am speaking. I'm not speaking about the contents of this interview and stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yeah, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That was my bottom line of my submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I understand your complaint, and I'll ask the Prosecution to explain. MR. DI FAZIO: With pleasure, Your Honour -- Your Honours. First of all, the interview in July of last year. Mr. Pantelic is correct that it was disclosed to the Defence late. I think I should take the fault for that. I was one of the parties involved in that particular interview, and I failed to chase up its translation and the obtaining of the transcript. And Ms. Reidy, in fact, solved that problem, brought the matter to my attention that it had been overlooked. And it was disclosed, as Mr. Pantelic says, in January of this year. That is an isolated example, and there is absolutely no practice whatsoever of the Prosecution concealing or failing to disclose relevant material or being tardy in disclosing relative material. In fact, the practice is quite the contrary. So he is referring to a isolated example. Secondly, what Mr. Pantelic didn't say to the Chamber is the reason why he should raise this issue at all. What is the consequence that has befallen the Defence? What's the problem that's occurred? Have they not had enough time to digest the material since the 18th of January? Knowing that Mr. Todorovic is not going to be giving his evidence for quite a long period of time, I am truly puzzled as to what consequence has befallen the -- the Prosecution. They didn't -- they didn't say or point to any particular consequence that results from this. So in fact, it's a complaint of the Prosecution not crossing its T's and dotting its I's and that complaint is not well-founded in the Prosecution's submission. And it's not for Mr. Pantelic to admonish or discipline the Prosecution. That is a matter that remains fairly and squarely with the Trial Chamber. Having said that, however, nothing could be further from the truth in terms of being tardy. It is entirely an isolated example. It's a matter that I regret. And as soon as we became aware that we hadn't in fact disclosed the material to them, it was done so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Does that mean that -- I may be mistaken, but if I remember at the opening of the trial, the Prosecution appeared to be saying that they hadn't made up their mind as to whether or not they were going to call Stevan Todorovic. Does this now mean that you are going to call him as a Prosecution witness? MR. DI FAZIO: Does the Chamber insist on my answering that question at the moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because of the complaint raised by Mr. Pantelic. MR. DI FAZIO: May I just confer a moment with my colleague?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, as matter of clarification, Your Honours, I said "18 of February," and my learned friend said "18 of January." I have a receipt of 18 of February -- MR. DI FAZIO: I don't quibble. February, February. That's fine. February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think that was the correct date when the document was given to Mr. Pantelic. All right. MR. DI FAZIO: He remains on our witness list and is expected to be called as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: Now, the other issue that was raised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If -- we should give a reasonable time. He should be called towards the end of the case to give enough time to the Defence, since they've said that they've just got the documents in February this year. MR. DI FAZIO: Mr. Pantelic well knows that weeks will pass, if not months, before Todorovic is called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And I think the point Mr. Pantelic made is also important that matters in those documents may be important for the Defence to have raised with the other Prosecution witnesses, which is actually allowed in cross-examination. MR. DI FAZIO: Certainly. Certainly. So let's hear what it is, if there is a complaint. I mean, that's what he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. He said so. And I would like the Prosecution to bear that in mind. MR. DI FAZIO: I do bear that in mind. I'm trying to make that point, if Your Honour pleases. I'm well aware of the fact that we should have disclosed the material at an earlier point. I don't seek to hide from that or escape that fact. It's regrettable that it was disclosed on the 18th of February. The point the Prosecution makes is okay, that's happened and it's regrettable, but what's the consequence? Now, if Mr. Pantelic can say, "We've lost -- there was a gem of evidence in that interview. The witnesses have disappeared. Our case has been damaged in some way," then let's hear it. But nothing has been said to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Maybe after he has digested the contents of the documents, he will be able to point out that. But still, that doesn't diminish his complaint, the value of his complaint. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't -- I don't suggest that it's a desirable matter or that it's a trifling matter. I'm not trying to escape that. And I fully accept that it's a matter that the Prosecution needs to attend to. But it's one interview, and I think there are at least five conducted. It's -- in terms of its length, it pales into insignificance compared to the other recorded interviews. And furthermore, it is utterly and totally diminished in terms of significance by the volume of material that I've given the Defence in the proofing notes as well. The volume of material, the factual material, the amount of facts, the detail that is contained in the recorded interviews that were disclosed quite a considerable period of time ago, and the same material in the -- in the proofing notes that I have provided to the Defence - I'm at a loss for words - absolutely is just a mountain of information and material compared to this thin volume of a few pages from July. It was a short, short interview with Mr. Todorovic. And that's the important thing, I think, that the Chamber should understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: In terms of information, they've got a lot more from those recorded interviews and from that proofing notes than they got from that July interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, very shortly. Well, we don't have to see some kind of approach with the pussy foots around here. I was very -- first of all, I'm very glad to prepare a short analysis what is the impact of this particular interview in terms of preparation of defence, in terms of the, I would say, interaction with the other witnesses here and stuff like that. So Defence will prepare that accordingly from this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Provided you bear in mind that the practice of the Tribunal is that where disclosure is at any stage during the trial, reasonable time should be given to the Defence before that particular witness is called.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You've already said what you intend to do. Can we move on to the documents which we were supposed to receive from Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let me ask the registry assistant. Have they been properly titled? That was D11/4, D12/4, D13/4, the English translations. Mr. Lazarevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. First is D11/4. These are portions of the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we just have confirmations of the numbers that -- yes. Can we move fast, because we are really keeping the interpreters beyond their hours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to give confirmation that these exhibits, D11/4, D12/4, and D13/4 in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Prosecution did say they have no objection, so they are exhibits. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, the document D12/4 are portions of law of All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And D13/4?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: D13 is an Official Gazette of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, dated October 18, 1991, signed by Dr. Branko Kostic, vice-president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I see Ms. Baen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: This is just a one-minute issue. And I think it might be some good news as to shortening the trial. I was told that the Prosecution had been requested to do -- to call most of the witnesses that dealt with the primary school at the beginning of this trial so we could try to move things along and set up the videolink. There's only one witness left in the indictment, [redacted], which has not testified before the Tribunal yet. And in talking with Ms. Reidy, the last I spoke about [redacted] with her, she said that he did not want to appear. And so I would like to propose -- and I know that Rule 70 requires that I make some sort of request to take a deposition, but that's something that we'd like to do. If he's not planning on showing up, then I believe that we're entitled to rely on their witness list. And we would like his testimony presented. And it won't delay the trial. I will actually take one witness off the list. And I can go, or my co-counsel can go, and take the deposition and not delay the trial at all. We don't have to be here. So that's just something I wanted to bounce off the Trial Chamber, see what you think and see what they think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And you say the Prosecution are not calling him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: That's the last I heard. I don't know if that's the status or not. That's just the last I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would have appreciated just a little bit of notice on this, because I would have asked that this go into closed session because precisely one of the issues about this witness's attendance has to do with the publicity surrounding his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So I would suggest that maybe we could pick it up first thing on Monday, if you want, or I could put in a written filing with he Tribunal, explaining the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. What I will say is you can discuss whatever you can discuss as parties and then you come up with whatever you have to come up to the Trial Chamber later -- after we have completed the witness on the stand.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: That's perfectly fine, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: That's fine. I just wanted to let you -- I did tell Gramsci yesterday that I was going to discuss it, so I didn't mean to ambush you or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. So the proceedings will adjourn until Monday at 14.15 hours.
